paper_identity.paper_title: Agricultural Resource Depletion and Arising Concerns of Environmental Ethics in Punjab: A Dire Need of Rescue, Revival and Sustainable Development

paper_summary: This review synthesizes four decades of secondary agricultural statistics and government reports for Punjab, linking Green Revolution rice–wheat intensification, very high irrigation dependence (especially groundwater), and input intensification to groundwater decline, soil degradation, salinity and waterlogging in the south-western belt, and broader sustainability and ethics concerns.
study_region: Punjab, India (state-level and three agro-climatic zones A/B/C)
study_period: Primarily 1970s–2010s with statistics through 2013–14 where cited; tubewell series 1970-71 to 2008-09; groundwater decline rate referenced since 2004-07
methodology: Secondary data review and synthesis from Department of Agriculture Punjab, Statistical Abstract of Punjab, soil survey division, and cited zoning literature (no primary econometrics).
paper_type_rationale: The article compiles published government statistics and prior studies to narrate resource-depletion patterns and policy implications rather than estimating new causal parameters from primary field data.

limitations: Review relies on aggregated official statistics; zone-level rainfall and groundwater decline rates are not block-replicated causal estimates; some social and health claims are qualitative.

important_variables.significance: Quantified 0.94 m/year decline in the central belt anchors the groundwater sustainability crisis narrative.
98% irrigated with 73% groundwater share explains concentrated aquifer stress.
190%+ intensity is repeatedly tied to soil and groundwater over-exploitation.
Among the highest national fertilizer intensities, directly linked to soil degradation and yield concerns.
Extreme pesticide intensity statistic supports contamination and soil-health risk framing.

important_variables_narrative: The paper foregrounds groundwater table decline in the intensively irrigated central belt, the state's near-universal irrigation dependence with a dominant groundwater share, and extreme cropping and chemical input intensities as joint drivers of resource depletion. South-western agro-climatic dryness and brackish groundwater set up salinity and waterlogging risks under rice expansion, while fertilizer and pesticide loads underpin soil-quality and productivity concerns for district-level monitoring agendas.
